metadata.title: TLCTC npm Supply Chain Attack Patterns
metadata.description: Canonical attack path patterns for npm supply chain attacks, decomposed into TLCTC threat cluster sequences. Each pattern represents a structurally distinct attack archetype observed in real-world npm incidents. Patterns use TLCTC v2.0 cluster notation with v2.1 transit boundary extensions.

notation.dre: + [DRE: X] denotes Data Risk Event (C=Confidentiality, I=Integrity, A=Availability, Ac=Accessibility)
notation.recursive: [RECURSIVE] denotes cyclic propagation — the path loops back to a prior step

vector_definitions.update: #10.1 — Update Vector: poisoned versions pushed through an existing package's update channel. Affects consumers with permissive semver ranges.
vector_definitions.development: #10.2 — Development Vector: malicious dependency pulled during pre-deployment dependency resolution. Affects consumers who add the package as a new dependency.

structural_observations.canonical_chain: The #10 → #1 → #7 sequence (trust acceptance → install processing → payload execution) is the canonical post-boundary chain in every npm supply chain attack. The #1 step between #10 and #7 represents the richest and most undertapped control surface.
structural_observations.cluster_1_dominance: #1 Abuse of Functions appears more frequently than any other cluster across all npm attack patterns. Modern npm attacks work overwhelmingly by using legitimate functions for unintended purposes.
structural_observations.credential_duality: R-CRED applies universally: credential acquisition maps to the enabling cluster; credential use is always #4. Controls at the #4 boundary (hardware MFA, token scoping, publish approval) break every campaign regardless of acquisition method.

patterns.description: A malicious or compromised package is pulled during dependency installation. The base pattern: trust acceptance, install processing, payload execution.
patterns.mappingRationale: #10 fires at the Trust Acceptance Event — the moment the package becomes authoritative in the target's dependency tree. #1 records the package manager's legitimate processing (resolve, download, unpack) which prepares the execution environment. #7 records FEC execution via lifecycle hook or import-time side effect. Collapsing to #10→#7 hides the #1 control surface: namespace policies, install sandboxing, --ignore-scripts.

controlsByCluster.#10: SBOM maintenance, dependency provenance checking, staged updates with canary deployments, internal mirrors with review gates, lockfile-enforced version pinning
controlsByCluster.#1: Namespace/scope restrictions on allowed packages, registry allowlists, sandboxed install with no network egress, disable or audit lifecycle scripts (--ignore-scripts), resolver restrictions
controlsByCluster.#7: Application whitelisting in CI/CD, postinstall audit requirements, sandboxed build environments, code signing enforcement

patterns.description: Attacker phishes an npm maintainer's credentials, authenticates as the maintainer, and publishes trojanized versions of the maintainer's packages.
patterns.mappingRationale: #9 is the phishing step — human psychological susceptibility. DRE: C records credential acquisition with #9 as enabling cluster. #4 records credential use (R-CRED: always #4). First #1 records the legitimate publish API call. #10 fires at the TAE when consumers pull the update. Second #1 records install processing. #7 records payload execution. The #9→#4 transition is the critical kill chain: controls at either boundary break the chain.

controlsByCluster.#9: Phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2/WebAuthn), domain monitoring for registry typosquats, security awareness focused on urgency/authority bias
controlsByCluster.#4: Hardware-backed MFA on npm, scoped publish tokens (per-package, time-limited, IP-restricted), mandatory publish approval workflows
controlsByCluster.#1: Publish-side: rate limiting, anomaly detection on publish velocity. Install-side: namespace policies, install sandboxing
controlsByCluster.#10: Lockfile-enforced version pinning, provenance checking, staged updates

patterns.description: Attacker publishes a package with a name deceptively similar to a popular package, inducing developers to install it through confusion.
patterns.mappingRationale: The initial #9 reflects that the wrong package choice was induced through human confusion or deceptive naming — a distinct control surface (developer verification, namespace reservation, review friction) from the #10 trust boundary that follows. The developer's decision to install the typosquat is a social engineering outcome; the TAE fires when the package is actually accepted into the dependency tree. #1 and #7 follow the canonical install chain.

controlsByCluster.#9: Namespace reservation/squatting prevention, IDE/CLI warnings for similar package names, mandatory peer review for new dependencies, developer awareness training
controlsByCluster.#10: Package provenance verification, download count and age heuristics, dependency review tools

patterns.description: End-to-end chain from malicious package installation through credential theft and lateral abuse. Extends the canonical chain with post-execution exploitation.
patterns.mappingRationale: Extends NPM-PAT-001 with post-execution exploitation. After #7 (payload execution), #1 records credential harvesting via legitimate filesystem/environment APIs (DRE: C). #4 records use of stolen credentials to authenticate to other services. Final #1 records abuse of those services' APIs for data exfiltration and/or further compromise (DRE: C, I). Note three structurally distinct #1 steps with different control surfaces: install processing, credential harvesting, and API abuse.

controlsByCluster.#1: Install processing: sandboxing, --ignore-scripts. Credential harvesting: filesystem permissions, credential isolation, vault-based secret management. API abuse: egress filtering, network segmentation
controlsByCluster.#4: Short-lived scoped tokens, separate build/publish credentials, MFA re-verification

patterns.description: Recursive supply chain propagation: the payload steals npm credentials, injects itself into all of the victim's packages, and publishes new versions — making each victim a new distribution node.
patterns.mappingRationale: The most complex npm attack pattern. After the canonical #10→#1→#7 chain, the worm harvests credentials (#1, DRE: C), runs secondary tools (#7, e.g. TruffleHog), scans for more secrets (#1, DRE: C), authenticates as the victim (#4), and publishes poisoned versions of the victim's packages (#1, DRE: I). Each poisoned package creates a new #10 TAE for downstream consumers, and the chain recurses. The [RECURSIVE] marker indicates cyclic propagation — each depth produces new propagation layers. The conventional linear model of supply chain risk fails; the exponential topology must be modeled explicitly.

controlsByCluster.#10: Lockfile pinning (breaks propagation chain), provenance checking, staged updates
controlsByCluster.#1: Install: sandboxing, --ignore-scripts. Credential sweep: filesystem permissions, credential isolation, vault storage. Publish: rate limiting, anomaly detection on mass publication
controlsByCluster.#7: Application whitelisting (blocks secondary tool download), sandboxed build environments
controlsByCluster.#4: Short-lived tokens, IP-restricted publish tokens, MFA on every publish action, publish approval workflows
